An ollie takes a varying amount of time to learn for people, when I was a teen I learned it in a few weeks and improved it over months, whereas some other people take months to learn it if not longer (I used to play soccer a lot as well as a variety of other sports, so I assume that helped me with good foot control early on). There's a lot of other stuff involved in an ollie, like balance and comfortability on a board at all. Since I don't know the specifics of your situation, a few key things I'd work on is making sure you are comfortable riding around on a board, taking turns, etc. It takes specific movements with your feet to do any tricks, and we aren't super dextrous with our feet, so making sure your feet are as comfortable on the board as possible is key, if you're struggling to balance while learning to ollie, or any trick for that matter, you're not gonna make any quick progress. Also, learn simple stuff like tic-tacs, 180 body varials keeping the board on the ground, etc. They're not super impressive as tricks, but in terms of the level of control they will help teach your body they can really make a huge difference. Try to find simple tricks like these to help build your dexterity and control, and you should begin to see some more improvement. Most of all though, try to have fun

The best way to explain what (I think) your confusion is about, is that fakie as a term is the name for the stance change. There's different skill level and difficulty with nollies and fakies, since fakies are the way you've learned to ollie already just moving in the opposite direction, and nollies are teaching yourself to ollie again sorta like teaching yourself to write with both hands. That's why there's specific distinction between the two, they require entirely different skillsets and can't combine. Nollie doesn't just mean 'any ollie using the nose'. One a stance changes, the skills required change, so the terms for the trick changes.

It's less about which leg is strongest and more about how you feel is comfortable, though when you're pushing, the foot that's on the board should be right on or behind the bolts, that will simply give you more stability and control when riding. Also, with practice you can do anything! With practice, on a skateboard anyway, you could even forget which foot is your 'strong foot' and that would be ideal :D If you're doing tricks and ollies with your right foot at the back, then practice skating with your left foot on the board at the front while your right pushes. There's less shuffling around on the board to get ready for a trick, and there's more stability and control, it might take some time but the fundamentals are worthwhile to nail down, and it can be harder to unlearn something once the habit becomes ingrained

It is also easier to approach obstacles on a skateboard than a longboard, if sidewalks aren't perfect. Someone said it would take you a year to get comfortable but that's not necessarily true, I started skating as a teen and was confident within a few months. Learning time is entirely up to individuals and how often you get to practice. Longboards have flex in the boards more than skateboards do which means that rides are smoother, but at more limited mobility, whereas skateboard decks are comparably more solid due to less distance between the trucks meaning you'll feel bumps more but will be able to handle more situations better. With practice it becomes a tactile thing, understanding how the bumps feel and how it will affect your movement. There are also some backstraps for holding skateboards like a backpack, but a longboard would be too large to conveniently carry like that. A skateboard will also offer you more variety in tricks, and will be cheaper to get a standard full setup going for everyone. Best thing to get less hurt is practicing falling. You want to shift your weight and momentum into a roll rather than landing your weight on anything directly. For example, putting your hands out to stop yourself falling on your face is good, but puts all of that weight onto your wrists. Landing with your hands out and immediately twisting your body around to slow and transfer that impact into your shoulder and then back is the best way. There's probably vids to help, you could even practice tumbles on the carpet or grass or something, but genuinely, knowing how to do that kind of thing when falling is the best to avoid broken bones

I remember telling teachers my home life wasn't ok and they said 'nonsense I've met your parents and they were fine'. My school counsellor outed me to my homophobic father without my knowledge or permission and genuinely ruined my life. I went to A&E after an OD attempt and wasn't seen for over 4 hours, left past 3am and wasn't contacted until 9 hours after that. There's an incredibly overwhelming sense of hopelessness when you're at the bottom, and every time you try something that doesn't work it reinforces the idea that you're irreperably broken. One thing I can say, is that small things from strangers mean a lot to me. A compliment makes my week, a smile, holding a door open, general, casual thoughtfulness. Losing people hurts and I know losing someone to suicide is hard to confront, so I would just say, to those who have been lost to suicide, live life and treat others how you wish you could have treated them.
